title: Baked Oats
subtitle: Oats blended and baked into a soft, cake-like breakfast
excerpt: Baked oats turn a bowl of porridge into something that comes out of the oven with a golden top and a soft, almost spoonable interior, halfway between a baked pudding and a thick pancake. The banana does double duty as sweetener and binder. Push blueberries into the top before baking and they burst into small jammy pockets during cooking.
sourceNotes: Baked oats gained widespread popularity in the UK through social media food content in the early 2020s, often made in single-serving ramekins or small baking dishes. The blended method, processing the oats before baking to get a smoother, cake-like crumb, became the most shared version.

recipe.freezeNotes: Bake, cool completely, then freeze individually wrapped. Reheat from frozen in the oven at 160 °C fan for 15 minutes or microwave for 90 seconds.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the quantities and bake in a larger dish for 30 to 35 minutes. Portion and refrigerate for up to 3 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Blend the batter the night before and refrigerate. Stir before pouring and bake straight from the fridge, add 3 minutes to the bake time.

content.text: Baked oats take the same ingredients as a bowl of porridge and turn them into something quite different: a soft, golden-topped bake that holds its shape, warms the kitchen while it cooks, and feels like a treat. The {{banana}} banana is the key, it sweetens the batter, binds it, and keeps the inside moist without needing butter or oil. Ripe bananas work much better than firm ones here; the riper and darker the skin, the sweeter the result. The {{baking-powder}} baking powder gives a small lift so the texture stays light rather than dense.
Heat the oven to 180 °C fan. Grease two small ramekins or a small ovenproof dish with a little butter or oil and place them on a baking tray.

Put the {{porridge-oats}} porridge oats and the peeled {{banana}} banana into a bowl. Mash the banana into the oats with a fork until you have a rough paste, it doesn't need to be completely smooth. Pour in the {{whole-milk}} milk, add the {{baking-powder}} baking powder and {{vanilla-extract}} vanilla extract, and whisk or mash until everything is combined. If you want it sweeter, stir in the {{maple-syrup}} maple syrup. The batter will be thick and not quite pourable, more like a very soft dough.

Spoon the batter into the ramekins and smooth the tops. If you're using {{blueberries}} blueberries, scatter them over the surface and press them in lightly so they're half-submerged. They'll burst and sink in during baking.

Bake for 22 to 25 minutes until the tops are golden and the centres are just set, a slight wobble is fine, as they firm up as they cool. Let them rest for 2 minutes before eating directly from the ramekin. They are quite hot inside.
Top browning too quickly: cover loosely with foil and continue baking until set.
Centre still liquid after 25 minutes: oven temperatures vary, bake in 5-minute increments until the centre is set. A cocktail stick should come out with just a few moist crumbs.
Texture too dense: the banana may have been underripe and not sweet or soft enough to break down properly. Use a very ripe banana next time.
Sticking to the ramekin: grease more thoroughly, including the rim, before pouring in the batter.
Chocolate baked oats: stir a tablespoon of cocoa powder into the batter and push a square of dark chocolate into the centre before baking.
Cinnamon and apple: swap the blueberries for finely diced apple and add half a teaspoon of cinnamon to the batter.
Dairy-free: use oat milk or almond milk instead of whole milk. The texture is the same.
